title: BrightSpring Health Services Research Report
name: BrightSpring Health Services
tagline: BrightSpring is a home and community health company that KKR assembled from a pharmacy chain and a 50-year-old care provider. Specialty and infusion pharmacy now brings in almost 90% of its revenue, and the stock is up about five-fold from a January 2024 IPO priced below its range.

chapters.title: Origins: from ResCare to BrightSpring
chapters.lede: BrightSpring has no founder story in the startup sense. It was built by private equity. KKR and Walgreens Boots Alliance bought the PharMerica pharmacy business in 2017 and in 2019 merged it with BrightSpring Health Holdings, the former ResCare, a disability and home-care provider founded in 1974. The idea was to combine pharmacy with in-home care for complex, mostly Medicare and Medicaid patients and become the lower-cost alternative to hospitals and nursing homes.

items: Chairman, President and CEO. He leads the strategy of growing specialty pharmacy and home health while selling off lower-margin businesses.
CFO. She set out the 2026–2028 framework of 15–20% growth and has driven leverage down from about 3x to under 2x.
The private-equity sponsor and its partner. They bought PharMerica in 2017 and still controlled a majority of the shares after the 2024 IPO.
ResCare starts as a provider of residential and community services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. It later grows into home care and workforce services.
KKR and Walgreens Boots Alliance take PharMerica, a long-term-care pharmacy, private for about $1.4B.
The PharMerica owner acquires BrightSpring Health Holdings, the renamed ResCare, and the combined company becomes BrightSpring Health Services.
BrightSpring postpones its planned IPO, citing market conditions.
The IPO prices at $13, below the $15–18 range, raising about $656M from common stock plus $389M from tangible equity units (TEUs). KKR and Walgreens keep majority control.
BrightSpring agrees to sell its Community Living disability-services business, the original ResCare core, to National Mentor Holdings (Sevita).
It buys 107 home health and hospice branches divested in the UnitedHealth–Amedisys merger, for $239M in cash.
The $835M sale (before adjustments) closes, and the proceeds go mainly to paying down debt.
Q3 revenue rises 26% and adjusted EBITDA 42%. 2026 guidance goes up again, and the stock jumps about 7%.

chapters.title: Early challenges
chapters.lede: BrightSpring came to market as a heavily indebted, sponsor-controlled company that depends on government payers, so investors were wary. Tap a card to see how each problem has played out.

items: A pulled IPO, then a discounted one
The 2021 IPO was shelved, and the 2024 deal priced $2 below the bottom of its range.
The discount became the opportunity. Shares have compounded from $13 to the high $60s as the company beat and raised guidance quarter after quarter.
As a KKR buyout, BrightSpring carried heavy debt into the IPO, and leverage was 2.99x at the end of 2025.
IPO proceeds, EBITDA growth and the $835M Community Living sale brought net leverage down to 1.79x by September 30, 2026.
Most revenue depends on government payers, whose rates, audits and managed-care shifts BrightSpring doesn't control.
Selling Community Living cut Medicaid exposure, and its top 10 Medicaid states were about 6% of revenue in Q1 2026. Medicare home-health rate cuts remain a live risk.
The Inflation Reduction Act and generics
Medicare drug-price negotiation and brand-to-generic switches threatened about $600M of pharmacy revenue.
Management says it has cut the profit impact of the IRA to about $15M, because lower drug prices shrink revenue more than margin.
With KKR and Walgreens holding a majority, outside shareholders face the overhang of future sell-downs.
Part of the IPO proceeds paid to end the sponsors' monitoring agreement. Sponsor share sales remain a recurring supply risk for the stock.
The 2019 combination brought disability services, workforce programs, pharmacy and home care, with very different margins.
Management has narrowed the company to two segments, pharmacy and provider services, by selling Community Living and buying home health and hospice.

chapters.title: Growth
chapters.lede: Revenue growth now comes mainly from specialty pharmacy, especially oncology drugs with limited distribution, and from home health, where the Amedisys branches added scale. Profit is growing faster than revenue as the mix shifts and fixed costs spread.

chapters.title: Stock trajectory
chapters.lede: The stock listed in January 2024 at $13 and has risen almost without interruption as results beat expectations and the company sold assets and paid down debt. Hover over the line, switch to the S&P 500 comparison, or click an event.

events: The IPO priced below its $15–18 range. The first months were choppy.
The market rewarded the move to a simpler, less Medicaid-heavy company.
107 home health and hospice branches for $239M.
Net leverage drops sharply once the $835M proceeds arrive.
Revenue rose 26%, EBITDA guidance went up, and the stock jumped about 7% to around $64.50.

chapters.title: How BrightSpring makes money
chapters.lede: BrightSpring runs two segments. Pharmacy Solutions dispenses expensive specialty and infusion drugs, and Provider Services sends clinicians into patients' homes. The pitch is that one company can manage medication and care together for high-cost patients.

items.title: Specialty pharmacy (Onco360)
items.text: Onco360 dispenses oncology and rare-disease drugs that manufacturers restrict to a few pharmacies. In 2026 BrightSpring expects to join about 16–20 new brand launches, mostly in oncology.
items.more: Newer limited-distribution networks often have only one or two pharmacies, against three or more before, so each win brings a bigger share of a drug's volume. Onco360 says 88% of its 2024 additions were ultra-narrow or exclusive networks.

items.title: Infusion & home/community pharmacy
items.text: CarePathRx runs infusion and hospital pharmacy services, and the PharMerica heritage business serves group homes and long-term-care settings.
items.more: This is the part of the business most exposed to Medicare drug-price negotiation and brand-to-generic switching.

items.title: Home health & hospice
items.text: Clinicians deliver skilled nursing, therapy and end-of-life care at home. The Amedisys branches added about $76M of revenue in the quarter.
items.more: Management expects the acquired branches to add about $35M of 2026 adjusted EBITDA. The purchase-price accounting was still provisional at September 30, 2026.

items.title: Divested: Community Living
items.text: This was the original ResCare disability-services business. Selling it cut Medicaid exposure and debt.
items.more: It is reported as a discontinued operation, and 2026 guidance excludes it.

chapters.title: What management prioritizes
chapters.lede: BrightSpring's investor messaging comes back to the same five priorities. Tap one to see what it means and how it shows up in the numbers.

blocks.label: Priority
items: Treat complex patients at home or in the community instead of hospitals and nursing homes.
Home health and hospice grow through acquisitions and organically (+12%), and pharmacy services follow the patient home.
Be the pharmacy that drug makers choose when they restrict distribution.
Onco360 has joined 140+ launches and expects about 16–20 more in 2026, with oncology growing about 15%.
Keep the two segments with the best growth and margin profile.
The company sold Community Living for $835M and bought 107 home health and hospice branches.
Get the balance sheet down from LBO levels.
Net leverage fell from 2.99x at the end of 2025 to 1.79x at September 30, 2026.
Use automation in pharmacy and clinical operations to grow earnings faster than revenue.
Management pitched an AI efficiency push at a March 2026 conference. Adjusted EBITDA grew 42% against 26% revenue growth in Q3.

chapters.title: Why it's on the radar: the 13F view
chapters.lede: BTSG made the Insights tab because many of the tracked funds own it even though its total 13F footprint is small, and the holder count is rising. Here is who owns it and how that changed.

blocks.html: The standout: Viking Global, a fundamental long/short fund, opened a new ~$113M position in Q2 2026, about 0.32% of its long book. That is the only large conviction stake. Most other holders are quant and multi-strategy funds with small weights.

chapters.title: Future outlook: opportunities & risks
chapters.lede: Analysts are almost all positive. They see BrightSpring as a specialty-pharmacy growth story with a cleaner balance sheet. The debate is about how much of that is now in the price after a five-fold run, and how exposed thin pharmacy margins are to drug-pricing and Medicare policy.

items: Lowest target in Benzinga's Sep 2026 snapshot
blocks.note: Benzinga's Sep 27, 2026 snapshot put the average target at about $82.33, with a range of $77–90. MarketBeat (July 2026) counted 19 Buy ratings, 1 Hold and no Sells. Targets were set on different dates, before the Q3 raise.

opp: About 16–20 limited-distribution launches in 2026, in networks narrow enough to give each pharmacy a bigger share.
The CFO set out 15–20% growth for 2026–2028, driven by volume and new drugs.
The Amedisys branches add about $35M of EBITDA, and organic home-health growth is 12%.
With leverage under 2x, cash flow can fund specialty-pharmacy and home-health acquisitions, which management says it is pursuing.
More seniors with complex, chronic conditions push care and medication toward the home.
EBITDA grew 42% on 26% revenue growth, and AI and automation could widen that gap.
risk: IRA negotiation and generic conversions are about a $600M revenue headwind, and future rounds of negotiation could hit specialty drugs.
CMS can cut home-health payment rates, and analysts flagged that uncertainty on the Q4 2025 call.
At about 5% EBITDA margins, small changes in reimbursement or drug mix move profit a lot.
The acquired branches still need to be fully integrated, and the purchase accounting was still provisional at Q3.
KKR and Walgreens may keep selling shares, which adds supply to the market.
Much of the good news is in the price, and the stock is close to the low end of recent targets.

items: Drug-price negotiation spreads to more specialty drugs, CMS trims home-health rates, and growth slows to single digits. The stock re-rates toward the low $50s or below.
The business is fine, but after a five-fold run the stock needs another round of guidance raises just to stand still. Targets around $64 reflect that.
Growth of 15–20% continues, leverage stays below 2x, and tuck-in deals add modestly. The market pays a steady premium for visible growth.
Oncology launches and narrower networks keep specialty growing in the mid-teens while home health compounds. Margins expand.
BrightSpring becomes the leading independent specialty and home-care platform, and acquisitions plus operating leverage drive EBITDA well past $1B.
Clears up the acquired branches' contribution.
This is the first full-year outlook without Community Living, and a test of the 15–20% framework.
Each oncology launch won adds revenue that compounds.
The proposed rule usually comes mid-year and the final rule around November.
Sponsor share sales can weigh on the stock for days or weeks.

glossary: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, with one-off items removed. It is BrightSpring's main profit measure.
Debt minus cash, divided by a year of adjusted EBITDA. 1.79x means about 1.8 years of EBITDA would pay off the net debt.
Growth from existing operations, excluding businesses bought or sold.
The company's own forecast for the year. A raise means management expects to do better than it said before.
A business that has been sold or is held for sale. It is reported separately and left out of guidance.
Accounting that assigns an acquisition's price to the assets and goodwill acquired. It is provisional until finalized.
A pharmacy that handles expensive, complex drugs, often for cancer or rare diseases, that need special handling and patient support.
A drug the manufacturer lets only a few chosen pharmacies dispense. Being chosen is a competitive advantage.
Prepares drugs given by IV, at home or in clinics.
When a brand drug's patent expires and cheaper generics replace it. The price drop cuts pharmacy revenue.
BrightSpring's infusion and hospital pharmacy services business.
The long-term-care pharmacy business KKR and Walgreens bought in 2017 and built BrightSpring around.
Skilled nursing and therapy given in a patient's home, mostly paid for by Medicare.
End-of-life care focused on comfort rather than cure, mostly paid for by Medicare.
Residential and day services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, funded mainly by Medicaid. BrightSpring sold it in 2026.
Care delivered at home or in the community instead of in hospitals or nursing homes, usually at lower cost.
US federal health insurance for people aged 65+ and some disabled people.
Joint federal and state health coverage for low-income people. Rates vary by state.
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the agency that sets Medicare payment rates, including for home health.
The Inflation Reduction Act lets Medicare negotiate prices on certain high-spend drugs, which lowers prices from 2026.
Insurer-run plans, like Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care, that pay providers on the government's behalf.
A payer reviews claims after paying them and can claw money back.
Initial public offering. BrightSpring's priced at $13 in January 2024.
A hybrid security sold alongside the IPO that combined a prepaid stock purchase contract with a small bond. It converts into shares.
A listed company where one holder or group, here KKR and Walgreens, owns a majority of the votes.
Existing holders, such as sponsors, sell shares to the public. It adds supply, though the company raises no money.
Leveraged buyout: buying a company mostly with borrowed money, as private-equity firms like KKR do.
An analyst's estimate of where the stock will trade in about 12 months.
The average of all analysts' ratings or targets.
A quarterly SEC report in which investment managers with over $100M list their US-listed long equity positions.
